Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

request verb and noun

also ask for, make a request, at someone’s request, I would ask you to, beg

classical

Cic. Att. 1.9.2: petō abs tē ut haec dīligenter cūrēs
Cic. Fam. 9.13.3: petō igitur ā tē vel, sī pateris, ōrō ut …

petō, petere, petīvī, petītum

verb, third conjugation; aliquid ab aliquō, or ab aliquō ut + subjunctive · Conjugation on Wiktionary

ask for, request

The usual word for asking someone for something: petere aliquid ab aliquō, or petere ab aliquō ut …. Its first senses are to make for a place and to aim at, attack (Rōmam petere, caput petere); it is also to stand for office (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • rogō, rogāre, rogāvī, rogātum — ask (someone to do something)

    verb, first conjugation; the person in the accusative, with ut or nē + subjunctive · classical · Cic. Fam. 13.44.1: idque ut faciās vehementer tē rogō · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Rogō tē ut … is the commonest way of putting a request in Cicero’s letters. The same verb asks a question (rogāre aliquem aliquid; see question).

  • ōrō, ōrāre, ōrāvī, ōrātum — beg, entreat

    verb, first conjugation; aliquem ut + subjunctive · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 13.66.2: etiam atque etiam tē rogō atque ōrō ut … · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Warmer than rogō, and often paired with it. Its older senses are to speak, to plead a case, and, in Christian Latin, to pray (Lewis & Short).

  • rogātū (alicujus) — at someone’s request

    noun, fourth declension, found only in the ablative singular · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 1.9.2: Thyillus tē rogat et ego ejus rogātū · Declension on Wiktionary

    Rogātū meō, at my request; Lewis & Short calls it Ciceronian. Seneca says it with a participle: patre meō rogante.

  • postulō, postulāre, postulāvī, postulātum — demand, claim; ask as one’s due

    verb, first conjugation; aliquid ab aliquō, or ut + subjunctive · also used · classical · Ter. Phorm. 411: Quid est? num inīquum postulō? · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    A request made as of right, so firmer than petō: Cicero sets postulat beside poscere and flāgitāre (Lewis & Short). The thing demanded is postulātum.

Examples

  • petō abs tē ut haec dīligenter cūrēs.

    I ask you to see to these things carefully.Cic. Att. 1.9.2

  • hoc mihi grātius facere nihil potes, idque ut faciās vehementer tē rogō.

    You can do nothing that would please me more, and I earnestly ask you to do it.Cic. Fam. 13.44.1

  • patre itaque meō rogante … ad prīstinam cōnsuētūdinem rediī

    so, at my father’s request, … I went back to my old habitSen. Ep. 108.22

See also ask, question, please, get, pull request.
